In [[mathematics]], a '''universal space''' is a certain [[metric space]] that contains all metric spaces whose [[dimension]] is bounded by some fixed constant. A similar definition exists in [[topological dynamics]].

==Definition==

Given a class <math>\textstyle \mathcal{C}</math> of topological spaces, <math>\textstyle \mathbb{U}\in\mathcal{C}</math> is '''universal''' for <math>\textstyle \mathcal{C}</math> if each member of <math>\textstyle \mathcal{C}</math> embeds in <math>\textstyle \mathbb{U}</math>. [[Karl Menger|Menger]] stated and proved the case <math>\textstyle d=1</math> of the following theorem. The theorem in full generality was proved by Nöbeling.

'''Theorem:'''<ref>{{Cite book|title = Dimension Theory|last1 = Hurewicz|first1 = Witold|author-link=Witold Hurewicz|series = Princeton Mathematical Series |volume=4 |publisher=Princeton University Press |orig-year = 1941 |year=2015 |isbn =978-1400875665 |pages =56– |chapter=V Covering and Imbedding Theorems §3 Imbedding of a compact ''n''-dimensional space in ''I''<sub>2n+1</sub>: Theorem V.2 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_xTWCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA56 |last2 = Wallman|first2 = Henry|author-link2=Henry Wallman}}</ref>
The <math>\textstyle (2d+1)</math>-dimensional cube <math>\textstyle [0,1]^{2d+1}</math> is universal for the class of compact metric spaces  whose [[Lebesgue covering dimension]] is less than <math>\textstyle d</math>.

[[Georg Nöbeling|Nöbeling]] went further and proved:

'''Theorem:''' The subspace of <math>\textstyle [0,1]^{2d+1}</math> consisting of the set of points, at most <math>\textstyle d</math> of whose coordinates are rational, is universal for the class of [[Separable space|separable]] metric spaces whose Lebesgue covering dimension is less than <math>\textstyle d</math>.

The last theorem was generalized by Lipscomb to the class of metric spaces of [https://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php/Weight_of_a_topological_space weight] <math>\textstyle \alpha</math>, <math>\textstyle \alpha>\aleph_{0}</math>: There exist a one-dimensional metric space <math>\textstyle J_{\alpha}</math> such that the subspace of <math>\textstyle J_{\alpha}^{2d+1}</math> consisting of set of points, at most <math>\textstyle d</math> of whose coordinates are "rational"'' (suitably defined), ''is universal for the class of metric spaces whose Lebesgue covering dimension is less than <math>\textstyle d</math> and whose weight is less than <math>\textstyle \alpha</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |title = The quest for universal spaces in dimension theory |last = Lipscomb |first = Stephen Leon |date = 2009 |journal = Notices Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=56 |issue=11 |pages=1418–24 |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200911/rtx091101418p.pdf
 }}</ref>

==Universal spaces in topological dynamics==

Consider the category of [[topological dynamical system]]s <math>\textstyle (X,T)</math> consisting of a compact metric space <math>\textstyle X</math> and a homeomorphism <math>\textstyle T:X\rightarrow X</math>. The topological dynamical system <math>\textstyle (X,T)</math> is called '''minimal''' if it has no proper non-empty closed <math>\textstyle T</math>-invariant subsets. It is called '''infinite''' if <math>\textstyle |X|=\infty</math>. A topological dynamical system <math>\textstyle (Y,S)</math> is called a '''factor''' of <math>\textstyle (X,T)</math> if there exists a continuous surjective mapping <math>\textstyle \varphi:X\rightarrow Y</math> which is '''equivariant''', i.e. <math>\textstyle \varphi(Tx)=S\varphi(x)</math> for all <math>\textstyle x\in X</math>.

Similarly to the definition above, given a class <math>\textstyle \mathcal{C}</math> of topological dynamical systems, <math>\textstyle \mathbb{U}\in\mathcal{C}</math> is '''universal''' for <math>\textstyle \mathcal{C}</math> if each member of <math>\textstyle \mathcal{C}</math> embeds in <math>\textstyle \mathbb{U}</math> through an equivariant continuous mapping. [[Elon Lindenstrauss|Lindenstrauss]] proved the following theorem:

'''Theorem'''<ref>{{Cite journal |title = Mean dimension, small entropy factors and an embedding theorem. Theorem 5.1 |last = Lindenstrauss |first = Elon |date = 1999 |journal = Inst. Hautes Études Sci. Publ. Math. |volume=89 |issue=1 |pages=227–262 |doi = 10.1007/BF02698858  |s2cid = 2413058 |url = http://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1999__89__227_0/ }}</ref>''':''' Let <math>\textstyle d\in\mathbb{{N}}</math>. The compact metric topological dynamical system <math>\textstyle (X,T)</math> where <math>\textstyle X=([0,1]^{d})^{\mathbb{{Z}}}</math> and <math>\textstyle T:X\rightarrow X</math> is the shift homeomorphism 
<math>\textstyle (\ldots,x_{-2},x_{-1},\mathbf{x_{0}},x_{1},x_{2},\ldots)\rightarrow(\ldots,x_{-1},x_{0},\mathbf{x_{1}},x_{2},x_{3},\ldots)</math>

is universal for the class of compact metric topological dynamical systems whose [[mean dimension]] is strictly less than <math>\textstyle \frac{d}{36}</math> and which possess an infinite minimal factor.

In the same article Lindenstrauss asked what is the largest constant <math>\textstyle c
</math> such that a compact metric topological dynamical system whose mean dimension is strictly less than <math>\textstyle cd</math> and which possesses an infinite minimal factor embeds into <math>\textstyle ([0,1]^{d})^{\mathbb{{Z}}}</math>. The results above implies  <math>\textstyle c \geq \frac{1}{36}</math>. The question was answered by Lindenstrauss and Tsukamoto<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lindenstrauss|first1=Elon|last2=Tsukamoto|first2=Masaki|date=March 2014|title=Mean dimension and an embedding problem: An example|journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]|language=en|volume=199|issue=2|pages=573–584|doi=10.1007/s11856-013-0040-9|doi-access=free|s2cid=2099527|issn=0021-2172}}</ref> who showed that  <math>\textstyle c \leq \frac{1}{2}</math> and Gutman and Tsukamoto<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gutman|first1=Yonatan|last2=Tsukamoto|first2=Masaki|date=2020-07-01|title=Embedding minimal dynamical systems into Hilbert cubes|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-019-00942-w|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|language=en|volume=221|issue=1|pages=113–166|doi=10.1007/s00222-019-00942-w|issn=1432-1297|arxiv=1511.01802|bibcode=2020InMat.221..113G|s2cid=119139371}}</ref> who showed that  <math>\textstyle c \geq \frac{1}{2}</math>. Thus the answer is  <math>\textstyle c=\frac{1}{2}</math>.
